AD.ACCOUNT.STALE_ENABLED.title: Accounts nobody uses are still switched on
AD.ACCOUNT.STALE_ENABLED.whyItMatters: Every enabled account is a door into the network. Accounts belonging to people who left, or service accounts nobody maintains any more, are rarely monitored and their passwords are rarely changed, so an attacker who guesses or steals one is unlikely to be noticed.
whatToDo: Confirm with the account owner or their manager whether each account is still needed.
Disable the accounts that are no longer needed, and move them to a dedicated organizational unit so they are easy to review later.
Delete them after a retention period that suits your organization, typically 30 to 90 days after disabling.
For service accounts that must stay, document the owner and set a password rotation schedule.

references.label: Microsoft: Active Directory Domain Services documentation

AD.POLICY.WEAK_PASSWORD.title: The domain password rules are easy to defeat
AD.POLICY.WEAK_PASSWORD.whyItMatters: The domain password policy sets the floor for every account in the domain. Short passwords can be cracked offline in a short time once an attacker obtains a password hash, and with no lockout threshold an attacker can keep guessing passwords over the network without ever being locked out.
whatToDo: Raise the minimum password length to at least 14 characters in the Default Domain Policy.
Turn password complexity back on, or replace it with a longer minimum length plus a banned password list.
Set an account lockout threshold so repeated failed sign-ins are stopped, and pair it with a lockout duration your help desk can live with.
Test the change on a small group first, because raising these settings affects every user at their next password change.

references.label: Microsoft: Active Directory Domain Services documentation

AD.PRIVILEGE.EXCESSIVE_ADMIN_MEMBERSHIP.title: Too many people have full control of the domain
AD.PRIVILEGE.EXCESSIVE_ADMIN_MEMBERSHIP.whyItMatters: Members of Domain Admins can do anything in the domain, including reading every password hash. Each extra member is another account an attacker can target to take over the whole environment, and nested groups make this worse because the real member count is larger than the group appears to hold.
whatToDo: List everyone who is currently a member, including members inherited through nested groups, and confirm each one still needs that level of access.
Remove day to day user accounts from privileged groups. Give administrators a separate admin account used only for administrative work.
Avoid nesting ordinary groups such as help desk groups inside privileged groups, because it hides the true membership.
Review the membership on a fixed schedule, for example once a quarter.

references.label: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises (joint advisory)

AD.PRIVILEGE.UNCONSTRAINED_DELEGATION.title: Some machines and accounts can impersonate any user who connects to them
AD.PRIVILEGE.UNCONSTRAINED_DELEGATION.whyItMatters: A machine or account trusted for unconstrained delegation keeps a reusable copy of the Kerberos ticket of everyone who connects to it. If an attacker controls it and a domain administrator has signed in there, the attacker can replay that ticket and take over the domain. Nothing has to be exploited for this to be true: it is what the setting does. It can be set on a computer, on an ordinary account running a service, or on a managed service account, and the Account category column below says which kind each one is, because the fix differs.
whatToDo: Find out what the service actually does before changing anything. Delegation is switched on so that a service can pass a user's identity on to a second service, for example a web application reaching a database as the person using it. Turning it off will break that, so confirm what depends on it first and plan the change with whoever owns the service.

Prefer narrowing it to constrained delegation over removing it outright. Constrained delegation lets the account act for a user against a named list of services and nothing else, which usually keeps the application working while closing the exposure.

For a computer account, or an ordinary user or service account: open the account in Active Directory Users and Computers and go to the Delegation tab. Choose “Trust this computer for delegation to specified services only” and list those services, or “Do not trust this computer for delegation” if it turns out none are needed. On a user account the tab only appears once the account has a service name registered.

For a managed service account or a group managed service account there is no Delegation tab, so use PowerShell. To remove it: Set-ADAccountControl -Identity 'name$' -TrustedForDelegation $false. To move to constrained delegation instead: Set-ADServiceAccount -Identity 'name$' -Add @{'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo' = 'CIFS/server.example.com'}. Remember the trailing dollar sign in the name.

Protect your administrators separately, so that a machine like this cannot replay their tickets even while it is being fixed. Add them to the Protected Users group, or tick “Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated” on each administrative account.
Until it is resolved, treat each of these as being as trusted as the most privileged person who signs in to it, and keep administrators off them.

references.label: Joint advisory: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises

AD.PRIVILEGE.KERBEROASTING.title: Service accounts whose passwords can be cracked offline
AD.PRIVILEGE.KERBEROASTING.whyItMatters: These accounts run services, so they are registered in the directory under a service name. Active Directory is designed to hand any signed-in user a ticket for a registered service, and that ticket is locked with the service account's own password. An attacker with any ordinary account, even a brand new one, can therefore collect those tickets and then try to guess the passwords on their own computer, where no lockout stops them and nothing in your logs looks unusual. The whole attack needs no special permission at all. If one of these accounts is also an administrator, cracking its password hands over the entire domain.
whatToDo: Give each of these accounts a long random password, 25 characters or more. Length is what defeats offline guessing, and nobody has to type a service account password by hand.
Remove any of these accounts from Domain Admins and other administrative groups. A service almost never needs domain-wide rights, and those are the accounts worth the attacker's time.

Set the account to use AES encryption only, by ticking the two AES options under the account's Delegation or Account tab. Accounts left on the default still accept the older RC4 encryption, which is far quicker to crack.
Where the service supports it, replace the account with a group managed service account. The directory then generates and rotates the password itself and this problem goes away.
Remove the service name registration from any account that no longer runs a service.

references.label: Joint advisory: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises
Microsoft: Group managed service accounts overview

AD.POLICY.RISKY_GPO.title: Group policy is handing out passwords or privileges it should not
AD.POLICY.RISKY_GPO.whyItMatters: Group policy is stored as ordinary files on a share that every computer in the domain has to read, which means every person in the domain can read it too. Three things found there are worth acting on. A password saved by a group policy preference is scrambled with a key Microsoft published years ago, so anyone who can open the file can read the password. A powerful Windows privilege handed to a group like Authenticated Users or Domain Users is handed to everybody, on every machine the policy reaches, and several of those privileges let an ordinary account take over the machine. And a policy that switches the guest account on opens a way in that needs no account at all. The Issue column below says which of the three each row is.
whatToDo: For a stored password, treat it as already known. Change the password on every account it was set for, then delete the preference that set it. Finding and removing the file is not enough on its own, because anyone who copied it still has the password.

Replace that preference with something that does not store a secret. Local Administrator Password Solution manages local administrator passwords without putting them in a file, and a scheduled task or service can run as a managed service account instead of a named account with a password.

For a dangerous privilege granted broadly, find out which application asked for it. These are usually added for one piece of software and then left in a policy that applies far more widely than intended.
Then narrow it. Grant the privilege to a specific group containing only the accounts that need it, and link the policy only to the machines that run that software, rather than to the whole domain.
For the guest account, set the policy to disable it unless you have a documented reason to keep it, and check whether anything is relying on it before you change it.
Check the scope of each policy before changing it. This report reads what a policy says, not where it currently applies, so confirm in Group Policy Management which machines it reaches.

references.label: Microsoft MS14-025: Vulnerability in Group Policy Preferences
